new.title: Drink craft beer in a former church at Stanislaus Brewskovitch
new.desc: On Stadsgravenstraat a former church now holds a brewpub with its own 500 litre brewing kit. Stanislaus Brewskovitch pours its own craft beers, and the kitchen changes its menu with the seasons and suggests beer and food pairings.
new.tip: It is closed on Mondays and opens at 16:00 from Tuesday to Thursday, and at 13:00 from Friday to Sunday. Ask the bar staff which of the house beers is freshest and start there.

new.title: Start the evening at brown café Het Bolwerk
new.desc: Het Bolwerk, on the street between the Oude Markt and the Wilminktheater, is counted among the oldest pubs in the Netherlands. It is a traditional Dutch café with beer on tap, coffee and sandwiches, and it is popular with the city's artists and creative crowd.
new.tip: It opens around lunchtime from Tuesday and is closed on Mondays. Come before a show at the theatre nearby, when the bar is at its liveliest.

new.title: Tour the Grolsch brewery and taste at the source
new.desc: Grolsch is brewed on the edge of Enschede, and the brewery opens its doors for tours of about two and a half hours. You walk through the brewery and the bottling plant and finish with a tasting in one of the brewery's own cafés.
new.tip: Tours run from Wednesday to Friday and must be booked ahead. Visitors have to be 18, though those aged 12 to 18 may come along with an adult.

new.title: Find the Elderinkshuis, a survivor of the great fire
new.desc: The Elderinkshuis on De Klomp was built in 1783 as an inn for travellers, including those who arrived after the Espoort gate had closed for the evening. It came through the great city fire of 1862, which makes it the oldest building in Enschede apart from the Grote Kerk.
new.tip: It is a private clinic today, so admire it from the street. The Grote Kerk on the Oude Markt, five minutes away, is the other survivor of old Enschede.

new.title: Stroll the garden village of Pathmos
new.desc: Between 1914 and 1928 a whole neighbourhood was built for the workers of Enschede's growing textile industry, on land bought by the textile baron Jan Herman van Heek. The architect W.K. de Wijs modelled it on an English garden village, with small squares, winding streets, arcades and brick houses under red saddle roofs.
new.tip: Wander without a plan and look for the arcades and the little squares. Combine it with the Volkspark, which lies a short walk to the north.

new.title: Meet the giant sequoia in the Ledeboerpark
new.desc: This 16 hectare park began in 1880 as the garden of a textile family's villa, laid out by Dirk Wattez. It is named after Abraham Ledeboer, a manufacturer murdered in the Neuengamme concentration camp in 1944. Its giant sequoia was voted Dutch Tree of the Year in 2025, and the old Saxon farmhouse Lammerinkswönner stands on the eastern side.
new.tip: Look for the 1880 entrance gate with its two eagles. The park lies on the way to the university campus, so it makes an easy stop on a bike ride out of town.

new.title: Queue for a cone at Van der Poel in Hengelo
new.desc: The family ice-cream maker Van der Poel comes from Hengelo, and its salon on Bornsestraat scoops ice cream made fresh every day with natural ingredients. The strawberry is about 55 percent fruit and the bestseller is cookie caramel, with caramel made in-house. The ice cream has won five gold medals.
new.tip: The salon stays open into the evening, when the queue is part of the ritual. The family also runs salons on the Oude Markt in Enschede and in several other Twente towns.

new.title: Take lunch at Carelshaven, Twente's oldest hotel
new.desc: Carelshaven has welcomed guests on the Twickel estate just outside Delden since 1772, which makes it the oldest hotel in Twente. The restaurant cooks with the seasons and serves lunch, high tea and dinner. In fine weather the terrace looks out over the park garden.
new.tip: Book a table on the terrace and walk it off afterwards on the Twickel estate. On Sundays the kitchen serves a four-course surprise menu.

new.title: Stock up on rusks at the Bolletje shop in Almelo
new.desc: Bolletje, the name on the rusks on many Dutch breakfast tables, has its own shop on Grotestraat in Almelo. A small museum on the first floor shows old baking machines, biscuit tins, cake moulds and photos of bakers at the wood-fired ovens.
new.tip: The shop opens from Wednesday to Saturday and the museum is free for shop customers. On Thursdays and Fridays a guide is on hand to show you round.

new.title: Taste Othmar beer where it is brewed in Ootmarsum
new.desc: Ootmarsum has its own brewery on the Commanderieplein, where Othmar beers are brewed in copper kettles. The tasting room opens in the afternoon from Thursday to Sunday, and brewery tours and guided tastings run on the same days.
new.tip: Ask for a guided tasting to compare the range before you settle on a favourite. On Fridays and Saturdays the tasting room stays open until ten.

new.title: Walk through Stork's garden village 't Lansink
new.desc: The machine builder Stork wanted decent homes for its workers, so from 1910 a garden village rose south of Hengelo station, designed by Karel Muller and named after the farm that stood here. The old oaks on the central C.T. Storkplein were kept, and the hotel built there for the company's foreign guests is still a hotel. Most of the neighbourhood is a nationally protected townscape.
new.tip: Start on the C.T. Storkplein and drift along the streets around it. The Tuindorpbad, a swimming pond in an old sand pit, has been in use since 1923.

new.title: Step back in time at Het Stift in Weerselo
new.desc: A chapel here was consecrated as a monastery in 1152, at first for Benedictine monks and nuns together. Around 1500 it became a foundation for noblewomen, and the little church you see dates from about 1400. The Stift houses were pulled down around 1800 and rebuilt in 1974 on their old foundations, from drawings of around 1750.
new.tip: The hamlet is tiny and best enjoyed slowly, so park the bike and walk once round the church. The houses are private homes, so keep to the lanes.

new.title: Count the trees at Arboretum Poort Bulten
new.desc: The textile manufacturer H.J.H. Gelderman and his wife founded this arboretum near De Lutte in 1917 and had it laid out by the garden architect Leonard Springer. More than 1,000 kinds of trees and shrubs grow on its 8.6 hectares, with a strip of woodland and a landscape of ponds around it.
new.tip: Entry is free. Come back in a different season, as the collection looks different in spring blossom and in autumn colour.

new.title: Ride a 1930 roller coaster at De Waarbeek
new.desc: De Waarbeek opened in 1924 as a tea house on the edge of Hengelo and grew into a family amusement park. Its Rodelbaan has run since 1930, when the park built it from old Enschede tram rails. It is one of the oldest steel roller coasters in the world still working.
new.tip: The park is a gentle one that suits families with younger children. It is open from spring to autumn, so check the calendar before you set off.

new.title: Climb the Kuiperberg above Ootmarsum
new.desc: Just west of Ootmarsum the Kuiperberg rises to 71 metres, high ground by Dutch standards, on the ridge the ice pushed up between Ootmarsum and Uelsen. On top stands an orientation table that recalls the festivities of the ANWB touring club in Twente in 1922. The Jewish cemetery of Ootmarsum, from around 1786, lies on the hill.
new.tip: It is a short walk from the centre of Ootmarsum. Go towards evening, when the low sun lights up the Twente countryside below.

new.title: Trace the brooks to their springs in the Springendal
new.desc: North of Ootmarsum groundwater seeps out of the ice-pushed ridge into three spring ponds, which feed three brooks. Around them lie 355 hectares of hills, heath, juniper, burial mounds and small old fields. Between 2019 and 2021 gold and silver coins and jewellery from the 6th and 7th centuries were found here, at a site of offerings to pre-Christian gods.
new.tip: Wear sturdy shoes, as the paths along the brooks can be muddy. The spring ponds were restored in 2023 and are the natural goal of a walk.

new.title: Jump into the lakes of Het Hulsbeek
new.desc: West of Oldenzaal an old estate was turned into a 230 hectare recreation park in the 1970s. Sand digging left three lakes for swimming, surfing and fishing, with walking and cycling routes and a mountain bike course around them.
new.tip: On hot weekends much of Twente comes here, so arrive early for a good spot by the water. In late August hot-air balloons lift off from the park during Twente Ballooning.

new.title: Cross the heath of the Buurserzand
new.desc: Between Haaksbergen and Enschede lies a nature reserve of about 455 hectares with heath, pools, old juniper bushes and little drift-sand hills. Natuurmonumenten looks after it, and from May to November Hereford cattle graze the heath to keep it open.
new.tip: Start at the De Wakel information centre on Stendermolenweg, where a walk of about 5 km passes the historic farm De Bommelas. The heather blooms in summer, and deer are easiest to spot early in the morning or at sunset.

new.title: Look for cranes on the bog of the Engbertsdijksvenen
new.desc: Near Kloosterhaar, north of Almelo, about 1,000 hectares remain of the peat bog that once covered the north-east of the country. It holds 17 of the 25 hectares of living raised bog left in the Netherlands. Cranes, bluethroats, adders and moor frogs live among the heath and pools.
new.tip: The 5 km Heideroute passes a bird hide, so bring binoculars. Stay on the marked paths, as the bog is wet and fragile.
